There are legitimate complaints for sure, they are usually just something that only someone who already runs linux would understand (e.g. trust in Canonical, UI changes). At the same time, many of these people forget that the reason Ubuntu is so popular today is that Canonical pioneered many of the things we take for granted in the wider linux community today (e.g. ez drivers, gui installer).

I think most of the criticism boil down to jealousy of Ubuntu's popularity. Even if I think Debian is better, which is why I run it, there's no good reason for Ubuntu to receive the hate it does.

Ubuntu or Mint are pretty good places to start out. There's a ton of stuff out there on google whenever you run into problems and they have pretty active communities on their respective sites. In all honesty it's pretty easy and straightforward for most tasks. Like opening up a web browser and listening to music. Some stuff won't run, even with Wine. Like I remember Fortnite was a big one. Not compatible with whatever anti-cheat software it used. But there are a lot of games for it on steam now and it's in a better spot than it used to be.

Some of the big name specialty apps aren't available but you can still edit your photos, do some music production, edit videos just fine.

Honestly for me the best way is to just jump right in and do it, work your way through the problems. Not bad to plan ahead but there's so much information that will make it seem a little more daunting than it needs to be. You can very easily go off into the weeds, then into some other weeds and sort of drill down into any particular topic at a higher level of detail than you need to. This would be my suggestion for getting started.

Make sure there are apps that do what you need to do. Pick a distro out, I'd say Mint or Ubuntu. Download the iso. Either burn the iso to a dvd (kind of old fashioned nowadays - lots of computers don't have optical drives) or else get a utility like Rufus and use it with the iso you downloaded to make a bootable USB flash disk.

You can either totally wipe out Windows or dual boot. Make sure you have enough free space on your hard drive if you want to dual boot. The Linux installation process will guide you through this.

Once the installation is done, you should be at your desktop and everything should basically be straightforward. Most packages and apps will be installed from a package manager. If it's Debian-based (like Ubuntu and Mint) then you could use apt from the commandline, or there's a graphical frontend that will be easier to get started with called synaptic.

Apart from that, if you download software from a website that's not found in the package manner's repository, say, Chrome for example, you'll download a .deb file and that's the software installation package. You'll want Chrome if you use any pay streaming services like Hulu or Netflix from your computer.

Eventually you'll want to look around the file system, see where things are laid out. profile folders are in /home. Filenames and folder names are case sensitive.
Just install it, for the most part it should "just work". Consider reading this, if the terminal is scary: https://ryanstutorials.net/linuxtutorial/commandline.php
Ubuntu has the most documentation for beginners that's recent. Once you learn it you can switch to something else. I dual boot for my main machine mostly because of games.
Installing Ubuntu is easy enough, then you just learn as you go.
install it and use it. it's not rocket science.
